paragraphs.source_en: As I said before, when we first moved here, the vacant lot had no fence, so the gentlemen of Rakuunkan, just like Blackie from the rickshawman's house, would amble into this grove of paulownias to chat, eat the lunches they had brought from home, roll about in the dwarf bamboo, and in short do whatever they pleased. After that they began throwing rubbish there: bamboo leaves used for wrapping lunches, old newspapers, old straw sandals and old clogs; in short, anything that could be called worn-out generally found its way there. My master, who never worries about anything, remained unmoved by all this and lodged no protest whatever. Whether this was because he knew nothing about it, or because he knew and had no wish to interfere, I cannot say. But as these gentlemen continued to receive their education at that school, they seemed to grow less and less gentlemanly, and little by little they began encroaching on the place from north to south. If the word encroaching is unbecoming when applied to these gentlemen, I am quite willing not to use it, but there is no other word that fits. Like nomads moving in search of water and pasture, they left the paulownia grove and advanced into the cypress grove. The cypress grove stood directly before my master's sitting room, and no one but rather bold gentlemen could normally have taken such action. After a day or two, their boldness acquired the prefix extremely and became extreme boldness. The effects of education are truly terrifying. They not only pressed up before the sitting room, they even began singing there in front of it. What song they sang I no longer remember, but it was certainly no thirty-one-syllable waka; it was a far livelier song, one much easier for common ears to take in. It was not only my master who was astonished; even I was conquered by the artistic gifts of these gentlemen and found myself pricking up my ears. Yet, as I imagine the reader will understand, admiration and nuisance can sometimes coexist. That on this occasion the two should unexpectedly have become one still strikes me, even now, as deeply regrettable. My master too must have found it regrettable. He had no choice but to run out from his study and say to them, This is no place for you to enter. Get out. My master drove them out two or three times. However, since these were educated gentlemen, they naturally were not going to obey meekly over such a trifling matter. Driven out, they came back in; once in, they began singing that noisy song again or talking at the tops of their voices. And the conversation of these gentlemen was distinctive too, filled with expressions like you bastard and go to hell. Before the Restoration, such language is said to have belonged to the special knowledge of samurai servants, palanquin men, bathhouse scrubbers, and the like; now, in the twentieth century, it has supposedly become the sole language learned by educated gentlemen. Someone has explained that this is the same phenomenon by which athletics, once despised by ordinary people, has become so welcome today.

paragraphs.source_zh: 如前所述，在刚搬到这里来的时候，那块空地由于没有围墙，落云馆的那些君子们和车夫家的黑猫一样，悠悠荡荡地进入这片桐树林子里来闲聊，吃从家里带来的午饭，趴在矮竹丛里滚来滚去，反正想干什么就干什么。然后是往这里扔垃圾，什么包饭菜用的竹叶子、旧报纸，或者是旧草鞋、旧木屐，总之，凡是被称为破旧的东西，一般都是扔在这里的。一向什么都无所谓的主人，对此无动于衷，也没有提出过什么抗议。这到底是因为主人根本就不了解情况呢，还是明知道也不想干涉，这我就不知道啦。可是随着这些君子们在这所学校不断接受教育，似乎越来越不像君子了，他们逐渐从北往南蚕食这块地方。如果蚕食这个词儿用在这些君子们身上不太得体，我当然也可以不用，不过，此外就没有恰当的词儿啦。他们就像逐水草而居的游牧民一样，离开了那片桐树林，进军到柏树林子里来了。柏树林正好是面对主人家的客厅，假如不是相当大胆的君子们，按理是不可能采取这番行动的。一两天后，他们的大胆再加上一个“极”字，变成了极大胆。教育的功效真是可怕啊。他们不单是逼近客厅的正面，而且还在客厅的正面唱起歌来。他们唱的是什么歌，我已经记不起来，反正不是那三十一个音组成的和歌，而是一种很热闹的、俗耳更容易接受的歌。吃惊的不只是我家主人，就连我都被他们的艺术才能征服，不由得侧耳倾听。但是，我想读者也是理解的吧，所谓“叹服”和“惹人厌”，有时也是可以并存的。而不料当此之际，恰好合二为一，至今想起这件事，还感到不胜遗憾。主人大概也在遗憾吧。他不得不从书斋里跑过去，对他们说：“这里不是你们可以进来的地方，给我出去！”主人撵过他们两三次。不过，这些有教养的君子，当然不会为这点子事就老实听从的。撵走了，又进来，一进来就又唱起那闹哄哄的歌，或高声讲话。而这些君子们的谈话也与众不同，满口都是“你小子”、“去你妈的”之类的话。这样的话，在维新前据说本是属于武士的家丁、掌班的、搓澡工等人的专门知识，到了二十世纪的今天，据说已成了有教养的君子们所学的唯一语言了。有人解释说，这与过去为一般人所轻视的运动在今天变得如此受欢迎是同一现象。

paragraphs.source_en: My master again sprang out of his study, seized one of those most fluent in this gentlemanly style of speech, and demanded why he had come in again. This gentleman at once forgot such elegant phrases as you bastard and go to hell, and answered in rather low language: I thought this was the school's botanical garden. After warning him to be more careful in future, my master let him go. To say let him go sounds as though a child had finished teasing a turtle and released it, which is rather absurd. In fact, he had grabbed the gentleman by the sleeve and reasoned with him. My master supposed that after such a severe lesson, there would probably be no further trouble. But from the age of Nüwa onward, reality has always run contrary to expectation, and my master failed yet again. After that they would sometimes enter from the north side of the grounds, sometimes cut straight across from the front gate, or fling the front gate open with a clatter so that the household thought a visitor had arrived, while from the paulownia grove came a burst of laughter. The situation grew more and more ominous, and the effects of education more and more evident. My poor master, keenly aware that he could not cope, shut himself up in his study and respectfully addressed a letter to the principal of Rakuunkan Middle School, begging him to exercise at least some control over his students. The principal of Rakuunkan also sent my master a courteous reply, saying that if he would wait a little while, a fence would soon be put up there. A few days later, two or three workmen came and, in the space of half a day, built a square-latticed bamboo fence about three feet high between my master's house and Rakuunkan. My master was delighted, thinking that at last everything would now be peaceful. In truth, my master is a fool; such a trifling measure could not possibly change the behavior of these gentlemen.
